entries.title: Apache Spark vs Apache Flink: which should you use?
entries.summary: For most teams, Apache Spark™ is the better choice. Spark runs batch ETL, SQL analytics,...
entries.content:
How Spark Real-Time Mode changes the streaming decision, with latency benchmarks, a feature comparison and a guide to choosing an engine.

  • Apache Spark is the default choice for most teams: one engine runs batch, SQL, machine learning and streaming, now down to millisecond latency with Real-Time Mode.
  • In a Databricks benchmark, Spark Real-Time Mode matched or beat Apache Flink on p99 latency for stateless, aggregation and join workloads.
  • Flink remains a fit for specialized cases such as very large keyed state or complex event processing on an existing Flink platform.

For most teams, Apache Spark™ is the better choice. Spark runs batch ETL, SQL analytics, machine learning and streaming on one engine, and Real-Time Mode now brings Spark streaming to millisecond, end-to-end latency. Apache Flink is a stream-native engine that fits specialized event-processing workloads, but choosing it usually means running a second engine next to Spark.

The latency gap used to be the main reason teams added Flink. With Real-Time Mode, that reason has largely gone away, and the real question becomes how many engines you want to build, operate and govern.

Spark is a unified engine for batch, streaming, SQL and AI, and Flink is a specialized stream processor. Both are open source Apache Software Foundation projects with exactly-once processing, stateful operators and SQL APIs. The difference is scope.

Spark started as a batch engine and added Structured Streaming, which treats a stream as a table that keeps growing. The same DataFrame and SQL code runs as a scheduled batch job, a micro-batch stream or a Real-Time Mode stream. Flink was designed for streaming first and treats batch as a bounded stream.

This table compares the two engines on the dimensions that usually decide the choice.

Dimension Apache Spark Apache Flink
Engine scope Unified: batch, streaming, SQL, ML and AI data prep Stream-first, with batch as a bounded stream
Streaming latency Seconds with micro-batch, milliseconds with Real-Time Mode Milliseconds
Batch and large-scale ETL Industry default for petabyte-scale batch Supported, less common in practice
Languages Python, SQL, Scala, Java, plus Go, Rust and Swift clients via Spark Connect Java, SQL, Python (PyFlink)
Stateful processing Aggregation, deduplication, joins, transformWithState, RocksDB state store Keyed state, timers, disaggregated state (ForSt) in Flink 2.x
Complex event processing Custom logic with transformWithState Built-in CEP library and SQL MATCH_RECOGNIZE
Machine learning and AI MLlib, feature pipelines, vector search in SQL, LLM data prep Limited native ML, usually paired with another system
Lakehouse integration Native Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg read and write Connectors for Iceberg and other formats
Managed options Databricks, AWS EMR and Glue, Google Cloud, Microsoft Fabric AWS, Confluent, Ververica and others

Table 1. Apache Spark and Apache Flink compared. Sources: Apache Spark Real-Time Mode docs, Apache Flink 2.0 release and Flink CEP docs.

In Databricks' published benchmark, Spark Real-Time Mode matched Flink on stateless work and had lower p99 latency on stateful aggregation and stream-static joins. The benchmark code is public, uses customer-derived feature-computation workloads and runs at 10,000 records per second for 30 minutes, measuring Kafka input-to-output latency. Databricks summarized the results as up to 92% faster than Flink.

Workload Spark Real-Time Mode p99 Apache Flink p99
Stateless transformation 3 ms 3 ms
Stateful aggregation 14 ms 45 ms
Stream-static join 9 ms 95 ms

How to read these numbers: Databricks ran the benchmark. Spark ran on Databricks and Flink ran on AWS Managed Service for Apache Flink 1.18. The results compare Spark's worst run with Flink's best run. Treat them as evidence for these workload patterns, and test your own pipeline before deciding.

Production results tell the same story. MakeMyTrip considered Flink, chose Spark Real-Time Mode to avoid a second engine and cut P50 latency to 44 ms and P99 from more than a minute to about 500 ms. Coinbase and DraftKings also run Real-Time Mode in production. For how the engine achieves this, read Breaking the microbatch barrier.

You change the trigger. Real-Time Mode is a trigger on an existing Structured Streaming query, so the same code moves between latency tiers without a rewrite.

Real-Time Mode needs update output mode and reads from and writes to Kafka or a row-level foreach sink. Stateful operators arrive in open source with Apache Spark 4.3 and are generally available on Databricks today. On Databricks, it runs on classic compute or in Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines. See the Real-Time Mode reference for the full support matrix.

REPORT

The agentic AI playbook for the enterprise

Flink can be the better fit for a small set of specialized streaming workloads. Consider it when most of these are true:

  • Very large keyed state. Flink 2.x disaggregated state is built for state far larger than local disk.
  • Complex event processing. You need pattern matching across event sequences with Flink CEP or SQL MATCH_RECOGNIZE.
  • Event-time timers on the low-latency path. Your logic depends heavily on event-time timers, which Spark Real-Time Mode does not yet support in transformWithState.
  • An existing Flink platform. You already run Flink in production and the stream doesn't feed batch, SQL or ML.

If the stream also feeds analytics, ML features or lakehouse tables, Spark avoids duplicating logic, operations and governance across two engines.

Every second engine adds a second codebase, a second skill set and a second set of governance rules. Teams that pair Spark for batch with Flink for streaming often rewrite the same business logic twice and debug drift between them.

  • One codebase. The same DataFrame and SQL logic runs as batch, micro-batch or Real-Time Mode.
  • One team. Python and SQL developers build real-time pipelines without learning a new runtime.
  • One governance model. Streaming tables and batch tables share lineage and access control in Unity Catalog.
  • One path to AI. The same pipelines build ML features for training and online inference, as DraftKings does with transformWithState.

Pipelines can also be declared instead of hand-wired. Spark Declarative Pipelines manage dependencies and incremental refresh for streaming tables.

Databricks was founded by the original creators of Apache Spark and runs Real-Time Mode as a generally available feature, including stateful operators and transformWithState. It adds Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines, Unity Catalog governance and serverless pipelines. Code written for open source Spark runs on Databricks unchanged. To get started, follow the Apache Spark tutorial: Real-Time Mode.

In Databricks' published benchmark, Spark Real-Time Mode matched Flink on stateless workloads and had lower p99 latency on stateful aggregation and stream-static joins. Results depend on the workload, so benchmark your own pipeline.

Not only. Spark Structured Streaming defaults to micro-batch, and Real-Time Mode processes records continuously with millisecond latency. You choose per query by setting the trigger.

For most workloads, no. Real-Time Mode gives Spark millisecond latency on the same engine you use for batch, SQL and ML, so you run one system instead of two.

Flink can fit specialized workloads such as very large keyed state, complex event processing or teams that already run a Flink platform for standalone streams.

Yes. Most Flink SQL and DataStream logic maps to Spark SQL and DataFrames in Structured Streaming, and Real-Time Mode covers the low-latency path. Start with stateless and aggregation jobs, then move stateful logic to transformWithState.

entries.title: OpenAI and Databricks: Enterprise AI on your governed data
entries.summary: Greg Brockman, co-founder and President of OpenAI, has a simple way to describe AI...
entries.content:
Three ways to put enterprise data and context to work with OpenAI and Databricks.

by Harish Gaur, Sully Clark, Ankith Ede and Suman Koduri

  • OpenAI brings frontier intelligence. Databricks brings enterprise data, context, and governance. Together, they help enterprises deploy AI that understands the business and can act on it.
  • Three enterprise adoption patterns: accelerating work for business users with ChatGPT and the Genie plugin, coding with enterprise-level governance through Codex and Unity Gateway, and transforming business processes with GPT models and Databricks Apps.
  • Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and CEO of Databricks, and Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, discussed best practices for rolling out enterprise AI

Greg Brockman, co-founder and President of OpenAI, has a simple way to describe AI without company data: “it's like hiring someone with 20 PhDs and never inviting them to a meeting.”

Enterprises want to use frontier OpenAI models on the business data they already govern in Databricks, and they want to roll AI out to far more of their employees. OpenAI and Databricks formed their partnership to make that possible. OpenAI builds the frontier models, Codex, and ChatGPT that people use every day. Databricks provides the context those tools need to work inside a company: governed data, business definitions, and access rules. Genie Ontology is the context layer in Databricks that holds those definitions and shows how the company's data fits together, so ChatGPT using Genie knows what “revenue” or “active customer” means at your company before it starts working.

Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and CEO of Databricks, and Greg Brockman, discussed the shift from chatbots to autonomous agents, and what enterprises need to get real value from them, in a conversation released earlier this week. You can watch it below.

Most companies start with OpenAI and Databricks in one of three ways:

  • Accelerate work for business users
  • Coding with enterprise-level governance,
  • Custom agents that transform business processes.

Each one is covered below.

Historically employees who needed numbers to make decisions couldn’t write SQL, so they looped in analysts or pasted data into AI tools that didn't know the company's definitions. Waiting on analysts slowed decisions down, and answers built on the wrong definitions led to the wrong decisions.

Now, they can ask these questions themselves in ChatGPT using the Databricks Genie plugin. This lets a product manager ask questions like, “How is weekly active user adoption tracking against target by plan tier?” ChatGPT will use Genie to understand the company’s metric definitions, find the relevant data, run the query in Databricks and return results back in visual graphs and charts. The plugin runs on the Genie MCP. Where once decision-making was slow, now employees can act quickly and with greater confidence in the underlying data.

Genie uses Genie Ontology, the context layer in Databricks that stores a company's approved metrics, business definitions, and how its data fits together. Genie applies the company's own definitions, so revenue in ChatGPT matches revenue in the finance reports. Users only see data they already have permission to see, and each answer links to its sources in Databricks.

Because ChatGPT has the business context from Genie Ontology, it can do more than answer. Users can ask ChatGPT Work for recommended next steps and who should be involved, share findings through Slack or email, and carry out the actions they approve through connected tools.

To get started, install the Databricks Genie plugin in ChatGPT.

AI coding agents usually spread one team at a time, and leaders lose track of who uses them, what they cost, and where code and data end up. Databricks Unity Gateway makes it easy to manage this rollout allowing a company to give OpenAI Codex to every engineer while keeping visibility and control. Developers use Codex as they do today. Codex signs in with a Databricks credential, the OpenAI key stays in the Gateway, and every request is logged. Engineering leaders set budgets, review spend by team, and pick which GPT model handles which task.

To get started, install the Unity Gateway CLI and run ug codex. The steps are in Connect Codex to Unity Gateway.

Agents that could change core business processes often stall before production, because the data they need sits behind strict security and governance rules. On Databricks, OpenAI frontier models run next to that data under Unity Catalog governance. When Databricks serves the model, there is no external API key to manage. Teams can build and evaluate agents in Agent Bricks, or write them with the OpenAI Agents SDK and deploy them as Databricks Apps.

To get started, open your Databricks workspace, go to + New > App, and choose the Agent - OpenAI Agents SDK template. The agent quickstart walks through it.

Behind the three patterns is one partnership. Here are the key facts, how the platform fits together, and the other integrations available today.

Topic Details
What it is A partnership between OpenAI and Databricks that helps enterprises use OpenAI models and tools on governed business data and context in Databricks.
When it started September 2025, as a multi-year agreement.
OpenAI products involved GPT models, Codex, ChatGPT, and the OpenAI Agents SDK.
Databricks products involved The Lakehouse, Unity Catalog, Unity Gateway, Genie, Genie Ontology, Agent Bricks, Databricks Apps, and Lakebase.
Common starting points Answers and actions for business users, coding with enterprise-level governance, and custom agents that transform business processes.
Relationship Each company is a customer of the other. OpenAI is one of Databricks' largest customers, and every Databricks engineer is getting access to Codex.
How to get started Install the Genie plugin in ChatGPT, route Codex through Unity Gateway, or deploy the OpenAI Agents SDK template in Databricks Apps.

OpenAI models, Codex, and ChatGPT connect directly to Databricks, and several Databricks products run on OpenAI models. Databricks gets early access to new OpenAI models, and OpenAI models lead on OfficeQA, a Databricks benchmark for real document work.

ChatGPT is where employees ask questions and get work done, Codex is where engineers write and review code, and Databricks Apps hosts the custom agents and apps that teams build. OpenAI frontier models do the reasoning in all three. Databricks Model Serving runs GPT models next to company data, so teams can call them from SQL, notebooks, and agents without managing a separate API key. Unity Gateway routes every model request, sets budgets by team, and keeps an audit log. The Genie plugin answers business questions in ChatGPT and Codex and gives them the business context from Genie Ontology to act on: the company's definitions, its data, and each person's access rights. The Lakehouse stores company data under Unity Catalog governance, and Lakebase, a managed Postgres database, keeps memory and state for agents.

The two companies have also built these integrations:

Integration What it does
OpenAI GPT models on Databricks Recent OpenAI models, including the GPT-6 family and the open-weight gpt-oss models, that you can call from SQL, notebooks, and agents. See the supported models.
Neon plugin for Codex Lets developers create Neon serverless Postgres projects, run SQL, and manage migrations from Codex.
Databricks Agent Skills for Codex Official instructions that teach Codex to work with the Databricks CLI and SDKs.
Codex Data Science plugin Runs Codex data science workflows on the Databricks Lakehouse.
ChatGPT Data Analyst plugin Lets users create and edit dashboards in ChatGPT over data connected through Genie.
One-click ChatGPT connection Connects ChatGPT to Databricks without admin setup and applies each user's existing permissions.

We'll publish a separate post on each pattern over the next few weeks, with architecture details, setup steps, and customer lessons. Teams that already work in ChatGPT and Codex can start with the Genie plugin and Unity Gateway. Teams that build in Databricks can start with OpenAI GPT models there. The same Unity Catalog permissions and Unity Gateway cost controls apply in every case.

OpenAI and Databricks work together so enterprises can use OpenAI models and tools on governed business data & context in Databricks. OpenAI provides GPT models, Codex, and ChatGPT, and Databricks provides the data platform and governance.

Use the Databricks Genie plugin, which runs on the Genie MCP. A Databricks admin turns on Genie, and users then connect it to ChatGPT. Each person sees only the data they're allowed to see.

Codex sends its requests through Unity Gateway instead of calling OpenAI directly. Developers sign in with a Databricks credential while the OpenAI key stays in the Gateway. Leaders can set budgets and see spend by team, and every request is logged.

Yes. Agent Bricks lets you build and evaluate agents, or you can also write agents with the OpenAI Agents SDK and deploy them as Databricks Apps. No external API key is needed when Databricks serves the model.

Databricks serves recent OpenAI GPT models, including the GPT-6 family, and the open-weight gpt-oss models. The supported models list shows what's currently available.

See the Databricks Genie plugin at work inside ChatGPT.

entries.title: Dispelling LTAP myths
entries.summary: Reynold Xin's post "From monolith to Lakebase to LTAP" explained what LTAP is and...
entries.content:
The lake is the database's storage, not a replica of it. That is why Postgres stays fast, analytics stays fresh, and no CDC pipeline is needed

  • Lakebase's LTAP design makes the lake the database's storage, not a replica: one Delta or Iceberg table, one catalog, with Postgres caches and pageservers in front for speed.
  • Point lookups read Postgres heap pages and scans read Parquet, and every analytical query sees a consistent snapshot, including commits not yet in the lake.
  • Logical replication replays every change through a pipeline that must keep up, which makes it a costly way to build the lake copy.

Reynold Xin's post "From monolith to Lakebase to LTAP" explained what LTAP is and how the Lakebase architecture makes it possible: one governed copy of operational data, serving both Postgres and analytics, with no CDC pipeline and no second database.

Much of the commentary that followed read that claim through systems people already know. Four readings came up often:

  • “LTAP is CDC under another name”
  • “A single copy of the data can have only one physical layout, so either point lookups or scans must be slow”
  • “Iceberg or Delta tables on object storage are inherently stale”
  • “Postgres already provides the extraction path: logical replication”

Each of these myths rests on a wrong assumption about how Lakebase stores data. Let's take them one at a time.

The reality: LTAP keeps one durable copy of each table, in the lake. The layers in front of it hold some of the same bytes to make that table durable and fast, but none of them is a second database.

From the outside, LTAP can look like a familiar pipeline. Postgres writes rows, a process tails the log, the changes land in an Iceberg table, and analytics reads Iceberg. That pipeline is CDC. It is also the structure of logical replication, mirroring, and most zero-ETL products. So it is easy to classify LTAP as the same design.

To see why it isn't, it helps to be precise about what counts as a second copy. There are two different ways a system can end up holding the same data in more than one place:

  • Replication keeps two databases aligned by shipping changes from one to the other. Each side has its own catalog and its own timeline, and either side can be queried as a source of truth. If shipping stalls, the two copies drift apart, and nothing forces them back together.
  • Tiering keeps one database and puts a stack of caches in front of it. The caches hold some of the same bytes so reads are fast. If a read misses the cache, it goes one layer down and costs some latency. It never creates a second catalog, and if a cache is lost, the table is not.

So the test is simple: can this layer be queried, or failed over to, as its own database? If yes, it is a replica. If no, it is a tier.

By that test, Postgres has always been tiered. The WAL, the buffer cache, and the indexes all store bytes that overlap with the heap. Nobody calls an index a replica of the table, because it has no catalog or timeline of its own.

LTAP keeps that same hierarchy. It moves it onto object storage and lets a lakehouse engine read the bottom, durable tier.

Here is what that hierarchy looks like in Lakebase, following a write and then a read:

  • A write is durable when its WAL reaches a quorum of safekeepers. The pageserver then applies the log, keeps hot pages in memory and on local disk, and materializes data into object storage.
  • A read starts at the compute node, which keeps a buffer cache and a local file cache. Indexes, TOAST, and visibility maps sit on the same hot path. A page that isn't cached there comes from the pageserver.

Object storage itself works the same way. When you PUT an object into S3, it is stored more than once, often across availability zones using erasure coding. The API still names one object, and no sync job runs between the copies. Lakebase stacks the same idea in front of the lake: log, caches, pageserver, object storage. The extra files are how one table is made durable and fast.

CDC does create a second database. It decodes a logical change stream into a foreign schema, usually keyed by primary key, and upserts into a table the source never reads back. That second table can be queried on its own, and it can fall out of step with the source: types can drift, DDL can go missing, a replication slot can drop rows, and tables nobody selected never appear. The result is two catalogs.

LTAP has no second table to keep in step. There is no list of tables to opt into. A table that exists in Postgres exists in the lake, and the pages the primary serves are caches of that store.

The reality: two lossless encodings of the same rows can serve different access paths - heap pages for point lookups, Parquet for scans. Each query reads the layout that's fast for it.

Even if the extra files are a hierarchy, layout remains a separate question. Point lookups are efficient on rows, scans are efficient on columns. If there is only one encoding on disk, one of those access patterns pays in I/O. Calling the table a single logical copy does not change that.

That reasoning is correct, but it rests on one assumption - that one copy implies one encoding. It doesn't, as long as two formats can represent the same rows without loss.

So the question is whether LTAP's two formats are lossless:

  • The primary format is Postgres heap pages, which are well suited to point lookups and updates.
  • The second format is built for analytical access: Parquet behind Delta or Iceberg. Values are preserved, and the files carry enough physical metadata (heap block, offset, and MVCC versions) that the original pages can be rebuilt. Values that Parquet cannot represent losslessly are not coerced or dropped; they travel in an overflow field in the same table.

Because nothing is lost, the columnar copy can be the durable store in the lake, and the heap pages become a cache of it. Each access path then reads the format that suits it. Lookups hit 8 KB pages on the compute node, on local disk, and on the pageserver. Scans hit Parquet through an OLAP engine. Indexes remain in the hot tier; they are not transcoded into Parquet.

Postgres already works this way. It keeps two physical structures over the same rows for different access paths: a heap and a covering index. Nobody treats the index as a CDC replica of customer. 

SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 1
and 
SELECT count(*) FROM t
are two access paths over one table.

A narrower observation is valid. The columnar files from Postgres are heap-ordered: rows sit in page-number order, because the page is the unit rewritten on each compaction. That layout is efficient for reconstructing a page and for rewriting only dirty pages. It is a poor clustering key for 

WHERE order_date >= …
. If a warehouse query needs that clustering, it can be derived the way silver tables are already derived from any operational source. What is no longer required is a CDC pipeline whose purpose was to create the lake copy.

The reality: every analytical query reads a consistent snapshot. Commits that haven't reached the lake yet are read from the pageservers, so nothing committed before the query is missed.

Iceberg and Delta provide snapshot isolation on object storage, and object storage has high latency. So it is natural to conclude that analytics is always behind, that many small tables cannot stay fresh, and that a join across tables cannot be consistent. That description fits CDC ingestion into a lake.

It depends on one assumption: that a query can only see what has already landed in object storage. In LTAP, a query can also see pages that are not in object storage yet. That changes the answer, and it is easiest to see by following a query.

When an analytical query starts,

  • It asks Postgres for the current LSN. That is a metadata lookup.
  • It reads nearly all of the data from object storage: everything already materialized up to that LSN. An engine that does not share CPU with the OLTP node does this read.
  • It merges the rest from the pageserver. Pages that got committed after the last materialization come from the pageserver and are merged on top.

Postgres serves none of the bulk read traffic - it returns a number and, at most, those recent pages. The lake does not need to contain the latest commit for that commit to be visible. It needs to contain almost everything, plus a way to fetch pages that got committed after the last materialization. The LSN is the cutoff: it tells the engine how far the merge has to go.

The same LSN also keeps joins consistent. CDC applies table by table, so one relation can sit at a later slot position than another, and a join mixes two points in time. LTAP reads every table at a single LSN, the same kind of cutoff Postgres uses for REPEATABLE READ, rather than at whatever each pipeline last flushed. That LSN is a shared watermark. APIs for reading recent changes since a watermark are being developed both natively for Lakebase and as an extension for upstream Postgres.

Small tables are a metadata cost, not a freshness limitation. Iceberg's overhead is files and snapshots. For a relation of a handful of rows, that bookkeeping costs more than it saves, and layout does not matter for scan performance. Those tables stay in the page cache, participate in the LSN-consistent read, and skip the Iceberg commit.

This leaves two claims that sound alike but aren't:

  • "A long query doesn't see new commits" - true, and correct. A query that started at LSN X will not see commits after X. That is snapshot isolation, the same contract as REPEATABLE READ, not replica lag.
  • "A query misses committed data" - this would be an incorrect result: a query that started at X and missed a commit that was already durable at X, because it was still sitting in a CDC buffer. Merging recent pages as of that LSN is how LTAP avoids this case.

The materialized columnar snapshot can lag behind the primary by the most recent compaction interval, but the query itself does not. The fact that Parquet files may be several minutes behind does not mean a reader is unable to see committed data.

The reality: logical replication is a costly way to keep the lake in sync with the database. It replays every change, row by row, and needs a pipeline that has to keep up. Decoding the WAL in parallel doesn't get around this, because log records can't be processed independently.

A standard way to get analytics on fresh Postgres is to enable logical replication. Debezium, PeerDB, pgoutput, and similar tools start from the observation that the database already emits a change stream, and ask what storage format is needed in addition.

The question is whether a change stream is a good way to build a table in the lake. Two properties of the stream say it isn't: how much it has to read, and how much state it has to carry.

Logical replication reads every change

The WAL is a physical log of page edits, written so Postgres can crash and recover. Logical decoding turns it into row events in commit order. That conversion cannot collapse many updates to the same page into the current image of the page; every change has to pass through. On a hot page, Postgres may log the same 8 KB a hundred times between checkpoints. Logical decoding emits a hundred events, then a downstream job upserts them into Parquet by primary key. In contrast, a page-tiering path reads the page once. In the write-intensive workloads we have measured, CDC reads at least the WAL volume, while dirty-page compaction may read a fraction of it.

Logical replication carries state

A replication slot is a cursor into WAL that the consumer must keep advancing. If the consumer falls behind, WAL remains on disk until the slot is dropped or the disk fills. Logical decoding does not emit DDL, so ALTER TABLE, type changes, and renames either make events inconsistent with the current catalog or invalidate the slot. Tables without a primary key need REPLICA IDENTITY FULL. Because the pipeline is expensive, it is typically applied to a subset of tables. That is the opposite of every Postgres table appearing in the lake because it exists.

A related claim: logical decoding can be skipped and the WAL decoded in parallel

Pageservers already consume WAL, so a parallel log-to-Parquet path can look like a small additional step. It is possible in principle. It has not been built as a production extractor, and it is not the path LTAP uses. WAL records are ordered because later ones assume earlier ones. Visibility lives in pg_xact, the proc array, and the catalog at that LSN, not in the tuple. Independent workers cannot each decode a disjoint byte range and emit correct current rows.

What LTAP parallelizes is pages, not log records. The system asks which pages changed since the last snapshot (WAL summaries on Postgres 17+, or the pageserver's log-structured merge trees), and each dirty page is independent work. That set is partitioned, the pages are transcoded, and one Iceberg snapshot is committed. The log is how writes were made durable, and one way to discover which pages changed. The snapshot is the current pages, not a replay of every record that dirtied them.

None of this makes replication the wrong tool for its intended jobs: migrations, major version upgrades, and cutovers to a second Postgres. But using logical replication as storage produces a second source of truth.

All four myths come from the same misunderstanding: treating every materialization of the data as a second database.

LTAP keeps one logical table, and the lake is its durable copy. Heap pages, indexes, and caches are how Postgres serves that table at OLTP latency, much as a covering index serves queries over a heap. An OLAP engine scans the Parquet directly and merges in transactionally consistent changes since the last materialization.

None of these layers adds a second catalog or a second source of truth that can drift.

For a deep dive on how Lakebase's storage architecture leads to LTAP, see this post.

entries.content:
How unifying data governance and semantics prepares enterprise data for AI scaling.

by Renee Voves and Herman Lombard

  • Constellation’s team built strong data capabilities within their own domains, but questions that cross domains, like “How many customers do we have?”, need shared definitions.
  • Constellation is building a governed Enterprise Data Platform on Databricks, using Unity Catalog for lineage, access control, and shared business context.
  • On that foundation, the team is developing AI use cases for nuclear engineering, outage planning, and sales.

Constellation operates the largest nuclear fleet in the United States. For them, one of the hardest parts of preparing for AI wasn’t choosing models, it was agreeing on what the data means. Constellation’s team is building a governed Enterprise Data Platform (EDP) on Databricks to make data consistent and usable across the business, and its approach offers a practical roadmap for other enterprises.

Constellation is the nation's largest producer of clean and reliable energy, with generating capacity equivalent to the needs of 27 million homes and approximately 2.5 million retail customer accounts. That breadth of operations and customer relationships is why shared definitions and governance matter to their data work.

Constellation collects data from asset management, supply chain, commercial and trading systems, and operations across the fleet. These are feeding everything from near-real-time market models to nuclear telemetry. In a business where safety and reliability come first, getting definitions and governance right matters. That risk profile drives every architectural choice that follows.

Teams across Constellation built strong data capabilities for their own work. However, questions that spanned those teams still required additional effort to connect information and reconcile differences in how it is defined. Data sat in dozens of places, with no shared semantic layer defining what it meant across domains.

Constellation faced a problem that many organizations still struggle with: a simple question with no single answer: “How many customers do we have?” Retail keys on the billing meter, wholesale on the counterparty and the CRM on an account or user. Three correct answers with three different meanings. The issue only compounded as Constellation grew through acquisitions, including Calpine in 2026, which had 79 power plants across 22 states and 27 GW of capacity. A completely separate stack with its own definitions, warehouses and modeling conventions. The EDP suddenly had to absorb an entity roughly Constellation’s own size. Bringing meaning to data and governance is the shift Constellation is making as it develops the EDP on Databricks.

Constellation's answer is a governed EDP built on Databricks. The EDP is the shared foundation that connects previously siloed systems and provides the business with a single shared understanding of its data. It's the deliberate shift from many disconnected, well-built systems to a governed foundation where data carries shared meaning across the enterprise.

The platform decision itself took only weeks. Constellation chose Databricks because it gave them room to experiment, grow, and mature as they went and, just as importantly, because it could interoperate with their existing architecture instead of forcing a rip-and-replace. Three architectural pillars stood out:

  • Shared meaning as conforming semantics. Rather than forcing each domain onto one definition, Constellation’s EDP team works with business leaders to define governed, conformed entities - agreeing on what a "customer" means across retail, wholesale, gas and CRM - and replicate those definitions across the enterprise. On top of that, Constellation built a semantic knowledge layer that maps the business relationships - customer, contract, asset and how they connect across domains.

    The team uses Data Vault as their modeling method which is used selectively for critical, reusable entities that need to flex as systems change. Not every dataset is vaulted. The modeling choice is deliberate and depends on whether the entity will be reused, audited, or evolved over time.
  • Governance is the ownership model, not just access control. A major decision factor for Constellation was choosing a service that went beyond traditional access control to convey semantic meaning to its stakeholders. With that criterion identified, Unity Catalog was the obvious choice. Unity Catalog provides the lineage, fine-grained access and single permission model. Constellation went beyond the technical layer to answer the question that other platforms struggle with: who owns the meaning? With Unity Catalog metric views, it is even easier. Different data domains call for different access and governance controls. Constellation’s team designed the platform to support those requirements as it brings new use cases onto the foundation. Establishing internal approvals and governance became the trust anchor.
  • Multi-workspaces on one governed foundation. The same governed datasets, surfaced across separate workspaces and business semantics are defined once and consumed many times.

For Constellation, Databricks supports both data engineering and governance, giving teams a controlled environment to build AI.

On the same governed foundation, three early use cases are showing what’s possible across very different parts of the business.

Constellation is developing an assistant, built with Databricks Genie and governed through Unity Catalog, to help engineering teams find and use approved technical information more easily, reducing the effort involved in answering complex questions.

Planned outages are among the most complex operations Constellation runs. They happen for refueling, major maintenance, regulatory inspections, and equipment work. Each one brings large crews and many work orders together at one site on a tight schedule. Coordinating them means drawing on scheduling, work execution, and asset health data from different systems. The team is bringing that data together in Databricks to help planners analyze schedules and coordinate work, with decisions remaining with the outage teams.

In sales, bringing together relevant customer and commercial information helps teams prepare for conversations and identify growth opportunities. The team is developing AI capabilities on Databricks to make this information more consistent, accessible, and actionable - supporting outcomes such as prioritizing high-value opportunities and recommending the next best action. All of this is built on the same governed data foundation in Databricks, with appropriate data guardrails.

Constellation’s experience underscores that an enterprise data platform is as much about meaning and governance as technology. Its team is building the definitions, controls, and reusable data foundation needed to support useful analytics and AI across different parts of the business. Databricks with Unity Catalog makes the data trusted and discoverable for business users.

This governed foundation also enables data scientists to build machine learning and agentic AI solutions with Databricks, including Genie One and Genie Agents. The team is using these capabilities as it develops use cases in sales, maintenance planning, and engineering support.

Constellation is exploring Genie Ontology, a self-learning knowledge graph that adds business context and Unity Catalog Pages, which centrally manages business definitions in Unity Catalog. Together, these capabilities extend the semantic layer by making data more meaningful, consistent and easier to use.

Learn more about their story in this blog post by Constellation leaders Jay Cavalcanto, SVP & CIO and Vineeth Vijaykumar, VP - IT Business Management Office.

entries.content:
Faster data access with a Rust-backed Apache Arrow connector

by Jack Yallop

  • Streamlined data access: Eclipse modernized nearly 20 years of flight telemetry to give service centers and engineers faster access to vital information.
  • Improved performance & speed: Significantly boosted data processing speed, allowing large flight histories to be analyzed in minutes.
  • Reduced costs & complexity: Eliminated redundant storage and multi-step processing systems, cutting operational overhead and simplifying management.

As organizations in aerospace, manufacturing, life sciences, and other data-intensive industries modernize their operations, they are bringing more sensor, telemetry, and scientific data into data platforms. But much of this data remains difficult to use at scale because it lives in specialized or proprietary formats that mainstream analytics engines cannot read directly. This creates a practical industry challenge: teams must choose between building slow, memory-intensive custom transformations, maintaining specialized connectors, or adding extra decoding stages before the data can be analyzed.

PySpark custom data sources offer a simpler way forward. They let teams bring specialized formats into Spark using Python, without building a separate connector from scratch. For Eclipse Aerospace, a very light jet manufacturer and operator, partnering with Databricks offered a way to make nearly two decades of proprietary flight data more accessible to service centers and engineers without adding costly, always-on infrastructure. Databricks brought the serverless data platform and Spark integration, while Eclipse Aerospace contributed its existing flight-data decoders and aerospace expertise.

Together, Eclipse Aerospace and Databricks developed a more direct path from flight data to analytics, reducing the latency, duplication, and operational overhead of the previous multi-stage process while preserving the flexibility of Databricks Serverless.

Eclipse Aerospace relies on Databricks to store nearly 20 years of flight data, totalling more than 3TB. It supports its service centers and engineers with data from more than a million flight hours, sourced and verified across multiple sources, including: near-real-time satellite telemetry; large bulk uploads of full flight histories; and external data sources. All of its telemetry is stored in proprietary file formats that require custom decoders, which are already developed in multiple languages, including Rust and Scala.

Before the Pyspark custom data sources was available in Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS, the Eclipse Aerospace team had three viable options for decoding and loading its proprietary file type into Databricks:

  • Load the files as binary types and split using Python user-defined functions (UDF)
  • Use a custom decoder in Scala on dedicated compute
  • Decode files into an intermediary file type prior to loading in Databricks

For simple custom file types, UDFs are a natural option. They trade performance for readability. However, where the message format has variable length, UDFs pose a real risk of running out of memory on long messages and could not be used. The existing Scala decoder could be used to implement a native Data Source v1/v2, but using it in Databricks required dedicated compute. Users expected to be able to upload and view data quickly, which would require keeping this compute to be always on, representing a larger cost than the other serverless options. This left the team with the final option of decoding the files into an intermediary file format, in this case, Avro, via a Rust-based decoder on AWS Lambda.

This solution was low-cost, but it:

  • Introduced latency from the multi-hop ingestion pattern
  • Duplicated schema logic between the Lambda decoder and the downstream Spark jobs that consumed the Avro output
  • Cost the team pipeline observability; the Spark UI and job metrics only ever saw the world starting at the Avro landing zone, so engineers debugging a slow or failed ingest had to go find Lambda logs in a completely different part of the platform
  • Meant paying to store both the original binary files and their Avro copies

Databricks was already Eclipse Aerospace’s platform for storing and processing flight data. The deciding advantage was the combination of Spark-native execution, the Pyspark custom data source, and Databricks Serverless. Databricks Serverless automatically allocates and manages on-demand compute, so Eclipse Aerospace did not need to provision or keep dedicated infrastructure running. The PySpark custom data source made it possible to wrap the existing Rust decoder without building a JVM connector. Because decoding now runs inside Spark, the same platform provides the Spark UI, job metrics, and downstream Delta workflows instead of handing the critical ingest step to a separate Lambda pipeline.

Most data engineering relies on common data formats, but some of the most valuable data remains hidden in formats that PySpark cannot access directly, such as HDF5 for scientific data and industry standards such as ARINC 429 for aerospace data. Databricks Serverless gives teams a flexible way to unlock that data at scale, while Rust-backed implementations can deliver performance beyond a pure-Python approach.

PySpark custom data sources lets you define a read/writable file format in pure Python, usable like any other data source. Its main benefit is simplicity, letting users define functions to read and write in pure Python, as well as define important characteristics like parallelization. The Eclipse Aerospace team took this a step further: by building a Rust-backed Python package, it delivered twice the benchmarked performance of a similar PyArrow-based pure-Python data source. Compared with a native Python implementation without Arrow, it delivered nearly 20x the performance.

The following example code repository walks through a custom data source for ARINC 429. The accompanying code includes design decisions beyond the scope of this article, along with benchmark tests you can run yourself.

Apache Spark 4.0 shipped a Python Data Source API (referenced in Databricks documentation as PySpark custom data sources) that lets you register a custom format for batch or streaming data like:

Introduced in Apache Spark 4.0 and available on Databricks, the API is generally available from Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS and is also supported on Serverless environment 2 and later. Because the API is implemented in Python, it does not require a separate JVM connector or JAR.

The API is a simplified interface for creating native data sources, with the user implementing a few classes and registering them with:

These decoders come in two flavors: native Python, and Apache Arrow format, the latter being the much more performant choice. Apache Arrow is a "language-independent columnar memory format for flat and nested data," making it an ideal interface between different languages sharing data objects. The API takes advantage of this by allowing users to return 

pyarrow.RecordBatch
objects directly, and Spark will consume them as batches rather than materializing one 
InternalRow
per row.

This raised the question: could Python serve as the control layer, with Rust doing the heavy lifting of decoding while maintaining the Apache Arrow format throughout?

The architecture behind this is a single logical connector with a decode path that's almost entirely compiled code, and a Python layer thin enough that it makes minimal change to Eclipse Aerospace's existing Rust SDK. This thin Python layer is built with PyO3/Maturin as a standalone package, imported into pipelines and used just like any other source. To ensure the best performance and separation of concerns, the team followed a few architectural principles.

The decoder doesn't know Spark exists. The core Rust crate has no dependency on PyO3, Arrow, or Spark and only takes bytes, returning structured records. That allowed Eclipse Aerospace to port existing decode logic largely unchanged, as the SDK did not need to be rewritten for this, only wrapped.

Arrow is the only thing that crosses the foreign function interface (FFI) boundary, and it crosses it without copying. The Rust glue layer builds an Arrow 

RecordBatch
using 
arrow-rs
, then hands it to Python as a 
pyarrow.RecordBatch
via the Arrow C Data Interface. In doing this, there is no serialization step, as no bytes are re-encoded and no per-row Python objects are built. The buffers Rust allocated are the buffers Python reads.

The PySpark layer is intentionally lightweight. It parses options, decides how to partition (one 

InputPartition
per input in the reference example), and defines the schema. In PySpark custom data sources, 
DataSource
, 
DataSourceReader
, and their streaming equivalents all have to be serializable, so Spark can pickle the reader instance and ship it to a worker. By making the PySpark layer lightweight, the 
DataSourceReader
instance that Spark pickles and ships to a worker only ever holds plain Python state (file paths, an int for batch size). The PyO3-backed Rust object is constructed inside 
read()
, after the reader has already arrived on the worker. It's never itself part of what gets pickled.

The native code ships as a Python wheel, built with Maturin. On Databricks that wheel is a build artifact, attached to a job or notebook environment as a normal Python dependency. Because the implementation is compiled, version and architecture compatibility require care, though a proper CI/CD process can manage this as demonstrated in the example repo.

On Databricks Serverless, the runtime path is straightforward:

  • A proprietary telemetry file lands in cloud storage.
  • A Databricks Spark read invokes the registered PySpark custom data source for the custom format.
  • Spark running on Databricks creates a serializable reader containing the input path and read options, then schedules input partitions on workers.
  • Each worker constructs the Rust decoder inside 
    read()
    and passes the file bytes to the compiled decoder.
  • Rust returns Arrow RecordBatches through the Arrow C Data Interface, avoiding serialization and per-row Python objects.
  • Spark running on Databricks consumes the batches and writes the decoded data to downstream tables such as Delta.
  • Decode errors, bad records, Spark UI stages, and job metrics remain visible within the Databricks workflow.

This is the key difference from the previous design: the original file is decoded as part of the Spark read rather than being copied to an intermediary Avro landing zone first.

By replacing the multi-stage Lambda and Avro workflow with a single Spark-native read, Eclipse Aerospace made flight data available faster while reducing infrastructure, storage, and operational overhead. The new Arrow-native PySpark custom data sources connector also brings decoding into Spark, improving visibility into pipeline performance and allowing schema and data quality logic to be managed in one place.

Implementing the custom data source has significantly simplified Eclipse Aerospace’s infrastructure, and the effects show up in four distinct places: latency, cost, observability, and engineering time.

Latency. Collapsing a multi-hop pipeline (upload, Lambda, decode, write Avro, read Avro, load to Delta) into a single Spark-native read removes several network hops and several points where a file sits in a queue waiting for the next stage to pick it up. The new connector can process records within a minute of file upload including startup time and can commonly process large, multi-gigabyte batches in parallel in under two minutes due to parallelism.

Cost. Removing the Lambda hop and the Avro intermediary removed a whole tier of infrastructure Eclipse Aerospace had to run, monitor, and pay for. They no longer pay to store two copies of every flight, the original binary and its Avro conversion, which on almost two decades of retained flight history is a meaningful amount of duplicated storage. This means the majority of files remain in Glacier storage on AWS, with easily repeatable decodes if the original data is ever needed again.

Observability. Because the decode step now happens inside Spark itself, it shows up in the Spark UI and standard job metrics like any other stage of a job. Eclipse Aerospace uses custom "badRecordsPath," which mimic the CSV/JSON loader, to capture misformatted data, and maintains extensive data quality pipelines that capture statistics directly from the decoder.

Engineering time. Schema logic used to be defined twice: once in the Lambda decoder that produced Avro, and again in the downstream Spark jobs that consumed it. Any change to the message format meant updating both, in two different codebases, with the risk of the two definitions drifting apart. With a single, versioned connector, the schema is defined once, next to the decode logic itself. This also means the same architectural pattern, a thin Python DataSource wrapping a Rust decoder, is now reusable for the other proprietary formats Eclipse Aerospace supports, rather than something that has to be reinvented per format.

Eclipse Aerospace's experience shows how specialized data formats can be brought into Databricks without creating a separate ingestion platform around them. By keeping the decoder in Rust, using Python as the integration layer, and passing records through Apache Arrow, the custom data source reads original files directly in Spark and remains compatible with the flexibility of Databricks Serverless.

For teams working with proprietary or industry-specific formats, the reusable pattern is simple. Engineers can keep domain-specific decoding logic close to the source format, expose it through a PySpark custom data source, and let Spark handle partitioning, execution, observability, and downstream processing.

Looking to get started? Take a look at the following:

A PySpark custom data source is a user-defined Spark data source implemented in Python. It lets teams read specialized file formats as part of a standard Spark workflow without building a separate JVM connector.

The Arrow-native PySpark custom data source connector ingests proprietary flight telemetry into Databricks without relying on a multi-stage pipeline, dedicated always-on compute, or duplicate Avro copies of the original files.

Databricks Serverless is a fully managed compute service that lets you run workloads without provisioning or managing any infrastructure in your cloud account. Databricks automatically allocates, scales, and optimizes the compute resources for you.

The connector uses the Pyspark custom data sources to run file-reading logic inside Spark on serverless compute. Python handles the control flow, while Rust and Apache Arrow handle high-performance decoding and data transfer. This allows proprietary files to be read directly without dedicated always-on compute or an intermediary Avro pipeline. PySpark custom data sources are available in Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS and above, or serverless environment version 2.

entries.title: How H6.ai builds AI-powered financial automation with Lakebase Postgres
entries.summary: Traditional accounts payable and invoice processing tools often force companies into a trade-off...
entries.content:
For H6.ai, database branching isn't just an infrastructure convenience. It is how we build AI-powered financial automation that customers can trust.

by Benji Borg and Mauro Pirrone

  • H6.ai gives every customer a dedicated Lakebase Postgres database, which keeps each customer's financial data isolated on a multi-tenant AP automation platform.
  • Copy-on-write branches save the exact database state behind any invoice issue, so the team can replay real customer cases without mocks and without touching live data or the ERP.
  • Disposable, schema-migrated branches and a panel of AI judges let H6.ai test new models and engine changes against real cases before they reach production.

Traditional accounts payable and invoice processing tools often force companies into a trade-off: moving quickly using AI automation and risk losing control, or maintaining tedious manual oversight. H6.ai was founded to solve this problem.

H6.ai automates accounts payable on top of a company's existing ERP. It reads each invoice, matches it to a purchase order, assigns its lines to the right accounts and checks it against the company's own policies. Our approach combines AI-assisted understanding with approved, deterministic and auditable policy execution. Our challenge was finding a backend solution that could support frequent regression testing at scale.

In this industry, no two customers look alike. Each has its own ERP, suppliers, purchase orders, chart of accounts and policies. Invoices range from a one-line service bill to documents with hundreds of lines.

And the data keeps moving. At 10 AM an invoice matches an open purchase order with enough quantity left. By the afternoon that order may be partly consumed, amended or closed. Process the same invoice again and the answer changes, even though our code has not.

That makes regression testing hard. When a result changes, we need to know whether our change caused it or the customer's data did.

Our engineering team needed a scalable solution that could isolate our customers' data and allow us to investigate errors. After learning about the lakebase architecture which separates storage from compute, scales idle compute to zero, and enables branching, we selected it as the core system of record for our platform.

Today, every H6.ai customer has a dedicated Lakebase Postgres database. It holds their whole financial context: purchase orders and suppliers synced from the ERP, the chart of accounts and dimensions, past transactions, and their H6 policies. A database per customer keeps each customer's data isolated.

It also allows us to freeze snapshots. A Lakebase branch is a copy-on-write copy of a database at a point in time. Creating one copies no data: the branch shares storage with its parent and only stores what changes on it.

When we find an invoice H6 handled incorrectly, we branch that customer's database and keep the branch as a snapshot. A purchase order that was open stays open in the snapshot, with the same remaining quantities and prices, even after the ERP closes it. The same holds for suppliers, accounts, dimensions, history and policy settings. We no longer try to recreate the conditions behind an issue. We keep them.

Every box in the shaded band is a branch of the same customer database. The harness branches the live database once to take a snapshot and never writes to it. Everything a test writes stays on its own run branch and is deleted with it.

Each test case in our harness pairs one invoice with one snapshot and the outcome we expect: which purchase order it should match, which accounts its lines belong to, and whether it should be held for review. A run has four steps:

  • Bring the snapshot up to date. Our database schema keeps evolving, so a snapshot taken months ago is behind the code under test. We branch the snapshot once, apply the current migrations to that branch, and reuse it for every run on the same code version. We migrate once and fork many times. The snapshot itself is never changed.
  • Fork a run branch. Each run gets its own short-lived branch of that up-to-date copy.
  • Process the invoice for real. The candidate version of our pipeline reads and writes the run branch as if it were the customer's database. It extracts, matches, classifies and validates the original invoice file exactly as it would in production.
  • Judge the result and delete the branch. We compare what the pipeline did with what we expected, then delete the run branch. The snapshot stays as it was, ready for the next run.

A test plan can mix cases from many customers, ERPs and invoice formats, each running against its own preserved database. Because every run starts from the same frozen state, the same test gives the same starting point today, next week and next quarter.

We don't mock the database or the pipeline. Isolation does that job. Everything a test writes (review items, validation results, draft documents) lands on the run branch and is deleted with it. A test never posts to the customer's ERP, and the live database is never written to.

This matters for a financial platform. We can test against copies of production customer data with the same code paths production uses, while the customer's books stay untouched. Branch management uses dedicated service principals with least-privilege access, and the branching guards refuse to touch a customer's live branch.

Checking that an invoice was processed is not enough. An invoice can be read perfectly and still be matched to the wrong purchase order, assigned to the wrong account, or processed in breach of the customer's policies.

So each run is judged two ways:

  • Deterministic assertions check the facts we can state exactly, such as the document's final status, the purchase order it matched and the totals.
  • A panel of AI judges built on models from different providers reviews the full outcome against the expected result and returns pass, fail or inconclusive, with its reasoning.

Together they tell us whether the outcome was right, not only whether processing finished. That lets us try new models, improve extraction, cut cost and change our matching and policy engines, and spot a regression on a real customer case before it reaches production.

We don't fix an issue and move on. We keep its database state as a snapshot, add the invoice and the expected outcome, and it becomes a permanent test case. As we onboard more customers, ERPs and invoice formats, test coverage grows with the complexity of the businesses we serve.

Lakebase Postgres gives us four things we rely on:

  • Isolation: one database per customer, as a multi-tenant financial platform needs.
  • Frozen state: a branch keeps the exact financial picture behind an issue, however much the live data changes afterwards.
  • Cheap, disposable copies: copy-on-write branches let every run start from a clean, identical state and be thrown away afterwards.
  • Schema-safe replays: an old snapshot can be migrated forward on its own branch, so it stays usable as our code evolves.

For H6.ai, Lakebase’s database branching isn't just an infrastructure convenience. It is how we build AI-powered financial automation that customers can trust.

In the future, we look forward to leveraging Lakehouse//RT queries on Lakebase tables which will allow us to run read-only analytical queries on Lakebase without copying data. This will allow us to get fresh analytics without a pipeline.

If you’d like to learn more about what we are building at H6.ai, visit our website. If you want to learn more about database branching with Lakebase Postgres, watch this video.

1. What is a lakebase?

A lakebase is a transactional database that keeps its data on the lake, for a modern, agentic app stack. Traditional databases run on single machines. A lakebase runs a stateless database engine and keeps data in durable cloud object storage, so compute can scale on its own and storage is used on demand.

2. What is Lakebase Postgres?

Lakebase Postgres is a fully-managed, serverless Postgres database integrated into the Databricks platform. Teams use it to build real-time transactional applications alongside their lakehouse data. It includes autoscaling, scale-to-zero, instant branching, read replicas, instant restore, high availability and native Unity Catalog integration.

3. Is Lakebase Postgres a good fit for AI use cases?

Yes. Lakebase serves as the backend for agent memory and real-time feature serving. Agents can store conversation state and long-term memory in Postgres, and models can read low-latency feature data through online feature stores powered by Lakebase. Branching also makes it easier to test AI systems. H6.ai, for example, replays real invoice cases against frozen database snapshots to catch regressions when it changes models or logic.

4. How does branching work?

A Lakebase branch is an instant, isolated copy of a database, much like a Git branch for your data. It uses copy-on-write: a new branch shares storage with its parent, and only changed data is written separately. As a result, branches appear instantly no matter how large the database is, and creating one doesn't slow down production. Teams use branches for development, testing and schema changes. They can also create a new branch from any point in time within the history window.

5. Does Lakebase Postgres support multi-tenancy?

Yes, in two ways. You can give each tenant its own database, as H6.ai does with a dedicated Lakebase Postgres database per customer to keep each customer's data isolated. Or you can keep tenants in shared tables and use PostgreSQL row-level security so users see only their own or their organization's data. Scale-to-zero suspends inactive compute, which keeps per-tenant databases cost-efficient.

entries.content:
AI agents can multiply your query volume. Lakehouse//RT keeps your bill from multiplying with it.

by JooHo Yeo and Kaitlin Baumgardner

  • AI agents can multiply real-time query volume almost overnight, and teams want to know whether their bill will multiply with it.
  • Lakehouse//RT is intentionally built to absorb that demand without a proportional cost increase
  • Customers that chose Lakehouse//RT over separate real-time serving layers report 6x to 10x lower infrastructure costs

AI agents are pushing the limits of data warehouses. A human analyst might run a few dozen queries in an afternoon. An agent can run hundreds per second, around the clock. And with growing demand for use cases like customer-facing dashboards that refresh in milliseconds and applications with embedded analytics, real-time workloads are quickly becoming a standard part of how businesses use data.

Most data warehouses were designed for human-scale query volume, not the sustained concurrency agents generate. And even when a warehouse can deliver low latency, the bill grows as fast as demand: 10x the queries could easily mean 10x the cost.

We built Lakehouse//RT not only to serve real-time workloads directly on the lakehouse, but to do so without growing your costs at the same rate as your queries. 

Most data warehouses scale capacity in step with demand: more queries, more compute, more cost. That works well for many analytics workloads, where query volume tracks the number of people asking questions. Real-time workloads are different. When AI agents and thousands of concurrent users all need answers in milliseconds, query volume can grow far faster than headcount, and cost grows with it.

Real-time workloads are also often spiky. The usual way to handle that is to overprovision: add capacity in large blocks and keep it running so latency holds up at peak. You end up paying for idle compute most of the day.

Lakehouse//RT flips the equation. Instead of scaling cost with demand, it scales efficiency. Its engine is architected to serve dramatically more queries on the same resources, so when demand doubles (or increases tenfold), your infrastructure keeps pace without a proportional spike in spend.

Lakehouse//RT achieves this by taking a different approach in four areas:

  • High concurrency support, so more queries share the same resources
  • Faster execution, so each query uses compute for less time
  • Autoscaling in small increments, so capacity follows demand closely instead of jumping in full-cluster steps
  • One system instead of several, so you stop paying for duplicate infrastructure and the work of keeping the system in sync

Organizations will not be able to outspend the demand curve. The only sustainable path is a system that does more per unit of compute.

Concurrency is where real-time costs usually grow fastest. Traditional warehouses can only run so many queries at once; the rest wait in line or trigger more capacity. Serving hundreds of agents then means running several clusters just to keep response times steady. That's true even when most of those queries are small lookups that don't need the horsepower.

Lakehouse//RT is designed to run far more queries side by side on each warehouse. In our launch blog we shared that we can deliver sub-100 millisecond latency at 12,000 queries per second, and we’re only getting better from here.

Each query also finishes quickly, so capacity frees up sooner for the next one. The same peak fits on far less compute, and the agents still get answers in milliseconds.

Customers are experiencing this on real-world workloads. Aurasell moved from several clusters at 200 queries per second to one small Lakehouse//RT warehouse sustaining more than 250 QPS, executing queries 4-5x faster while reducing costs by 10x.

Keep reading for more customer success stories!

Say you hire a contractor. One charges $20 an hour and takes 10 hours. Another charges $22 an hour and finishes in five. The first costs $200 and the second costs $110. You pay for the finished job, not the hour.

Compute works the same way: your bill is rate times runtime. Lakehouse//RT is built to finish real-time queries fast, including the steps around execution like planning, routing, and returning results. Each query holds compute for less time. Across millions of agent queries a day, that adds up.

Every warehouse eventually needs more capacity as traffic grows. What matters is the size of each step.

Traditional warehouses typically scale by spinning up whole copies of themselves. On a Large warehouse, that's another Large warehouse spinning up. While cluster-level scaling works well for steady analytics workloads, real-time demand is spikier. When a burst needs only a fraction of a cluster, adding a whole cluster means paying for capacity you don't use until the burst passes.

Lakehouse//RT can flexibly add capacity, even one node at a time, whatever t-shirt size you select. Real-time demand rarely arrives in cluster-sized blocks. A spike in agent traffic might need 10% more capacity, not 100%, and Lakehouse//RT can add a step that size instead of doubling.

Scaling in small steps without hurting latency is easier said than done. It's what Lakehouse//RT was designed for, and it lets capacity grow in step with demand instead of ahead of it.

Real-time used to mean bolting a separate serving layer onto your warehouse, such as Apache Druid, Apache Pinot, or a cache. That meant always-on infrastructure, a second copy of your data, sync pipelines, and engineers to keep it all consistent.

Lakehouse//RT queries governed lakehouse data directly, so as volume grows there's no second stack growing alongside it.

Aurasell's AI-native go-to-market platform runs agents that prospect, manage pipeline, and coach reps around the clock. Those agentic workflows depend on high query throughput, and Aurasell wanted real-time performance without moving or indexing data into an external system. With Lakehouse//RT, the team serves that workload directly in Databricks from a single small cluster.

"High query throughput is critical for our agentic workflows at Aurasell. Before Lakehouse//RT, reaching 200 queries per second required us to spin up several separate clusters, which added complexity. With Lakehouse//RT, a single small cluster easily sustained over 250 QPS while executing queries 4-5x faster. Beyond the 10x improvement in infrastructure and cost efficiency by consolidating clusters, the biggest win is architectural simplicity; we get the real-time performance we need directly in Databricks without having to move or index our data into external systems." – Srinivas Bandi, CTO, Aurasell

VisionHeight is a pre-attack intelligence platform that maps adversary infrastructure across the public internet in real time. Their previous real-time layer ran on Apache Pinot with always-on EC2 clusters running 24/7. After switching to Lakehouse//RT's serverless model, VisionHeight saw a cost reduction of more than 90%. On their heaviest query, Lakehouse//RT delivered sub-second response times, nearly 3x faster than Pinot. The entire migration took three days.
