entries.content:
Bring Genie into Slack to get governed answers, charts, and actions right in your flow of work.

by Toussaint Webb and Sydney Sundell

• Genie in Slack is generally available: DM Genie or @mention it in a channel to get governed answers grounded in your business context without leaving Slack.

• From answers to action: Genie updates documents and tickets through MCP connectors after you approve, and works with files and runs analyses on a schedule.

• Governed by design: Every question runs with the asker's permissions, so Unity Catalog and source permissions apply in DMs and channels alike.

Many business questions can’t be started and answered within the same conversation. A manager asks her team in Slack why revenue growth slowed last month across active customers. To answer, someone needs to find the right dashboard, check it against the number finance reported, and search last week's meeting notes for the explanation. Two hours later, they paste their findings back into the thread, but the conversation has already moved on.

The delay doesn't come from the question being hard, it comes from having to piece together data from multiple scattered sources. The revenue numbers live in your data platform, the explanation for the slowdown lives in documents and tickets, the definition of “active customer” varies across teams, and decisions happen in Slack.

Today, we’re making it easier than ever for teams to answer questions right where they start, with the General Availability of the Databricks Genie app for Slack. Genie now answers in the channel, thread, or DM where questions are asked, with the same governed context and permissions it uses directly in Databricks.

The Databricks Genie app for Slack brings the power of Genie directly into your Slack workspace. You can start a DM with Genie or @mention it in a channel, and Genie responds directly in the thread, with answers grounded in the governed business context you have access to through Unity Catalog and any outside tool source permissions.

Every answer cites its sources, so you can scan the context Genie used to compile your results without leaving Slack, or click directly on a source to explore deeper in Genie One.

Teams can work with Genie together in any channel Genie has been added to. Anyone who has connected their Databricks account can type @Genie, and Genie replies directly in the thread with a response. Genie will only read the context of the channels it has been invited to, and responds to each question within the context of the channel it was asked in.

Genie answers in the thread it's called from, so follow-up questions keep their context and move the conversation along. Responses are visible to everyone in the channel by default, giving the team shared context for decisions. For more privacy, admins can set responses to be private to the person who asked as the default for the whole workspace.

Each channel has its own configuration. You choose which Databricks workspace the channel connects to, and whether questions go to Genie One or to a specific Genie Agent. By default, channels use Genie One, which routes questions across Genie Search, Genie Agents, and more, for a comprehensive view of results across your data estate. For domain-specific channels such as "Product FAQs" or "Employee Benefits,” you can pin a curated Genie Agent to a channel, so answers stay scoped to that agent's data and instructions.

Users can work privately with Genie right from a DM. You can ask questions about your data, search the enterprise knowledge sources you've connected, see results as tables and charts, upload files for Genie to analyze and take action in other tools from the same chat. DM answers use your permissions and stay private to you, just as a chat would in Genie One or Genie Agents.

Of course, a trusted answer is useful only if someone acts on it. With Genie embedded directly in Slack, users can turn insights into work right from their Slack workspace:

  • Take action across your tools: Through MCP connectors, Genie can create or update documents, comment on tickets and update records with your own credentials. It prepares each change for your approval before it runs.
  • Schedule recurring analyses: Click “Run this analysis on a schedule” under an answer, or ask in your own words, for example "Send me this analysis every Monday at 9 AM." Results arrive in your DM.
  • Work with files: Attach a file for Genie to analyze, and get documents such as PDFs back in the thread.
  • Share charts in a thread: Genie returns visualizations directly in Slack, so the chart is ready when your team needs it.

These same capabilities empower AI cowork directly in Genie One, so you can orchestrate and review your workflows from whichever system you prefer.

Genie in Slack follows the same governance as every other Genie surface. Every question runs using the identity of the person who asked it, across Unity Catalog and each connected source, so Genie uses only information that person is allowed to see. In channels, answers use the permissions of whoever asked, and each channel can choose whether responses are shared with the channel or sent privately to the asker. Workspace admins can set this default for the whole workspace.

Admins can govern AI usage centrally in Unity Gateway, including MCP policies, cost controls, and monitoring. MCP policies decide which MCP servers and tools Genie can use, which users can access them and which actions require human approval, and traces record what Genie did and who asked for it. Workspaces that use Private Link are supported through context-based ingress policies.

Questions about your company's data and knowledge don't come up in isolation, so they shouldn't be answered in isolation either. The Databricks Genie app for Slack brings governed answers and actions into the conversation where your team already makes decisions, with no new tool to learn and no new permissions model to manage.

Get started today:

  • Admins: Install the Databricks Genie app from the Slack Marketplace and configure channels and response visibility. Review our documentation for more information.
  • Users: DM Genie or @mention it in a channel. The first time, sign in to Databricks and pick a workspace.

To learn more about the Databricks Genie App for Slack, join our webinar: "Just Ask Your Data: Bring Databricks Genie into Slack"

  • Admins: Install the Databricks Genie app in your Slack workspace.
  • Users: DM Genie or @mention it in a channel. The first time, sign in to Databricks and pick a workspace.

Yes. Genie One is the default. It looks across your entire data estate to answer each question. You can also pin a conversation or channel to a specific Genie Agent. Questions are then sent to that agent through the Genie Agentic API, so answers stay scoped to that agent's curated data and instructions.

Genie in Slack does much more than answer questions. You can:

  • Discover and visualize insights: Get answers, tables, and charts from your Databricks data in a DM or channel thread.
  • Search your company's knowledge: Pull in context from connected sources such as Google Drive, Confluence, or Jira.
  • Take action in other tools: Create or update a document, comment on a ticket, or update a record through MCP connectors. Genie asks for your approval before it makes a change.
  • Schedule recurring analyses: Run an analysis on a schedule and get the results in your DM.
  • Work with files: Upload a file for Genie to analyze, and get documents such as PDFs back in the thread.
  • Pick the right expert: Use Genie One across your whole data estate, or pin a conversation or channel to a specific Genie Agent.
  • Get notifications: Receive Databricks platform notifications in Slack (documentation).
  • Give feedback: Rate answers with a thumbs up or down to help improve Genie.

You have two options:

  • In Databricks: Create a scheduled task in Genie One and choose Slack as where results are delivered.

Either way, results arrive in your Genie DM. You need to sign in to the Genie app from a DM once before results can be delivered.

Questions are processed inside your Databricks workspace. The service that routes messages between Slack and Databricks doesn't store questions or answers.

entries.title: How Block powers collaborative AI agents with Buzz and Unity Gateway
entries.summary: Inside Block, Buzz brings employees and AI agents into a shared workspace. With Databricks...
entries.content:
by Bradley Axen, Brandon Kvarda, Julia Powell and Kelly Albano

Inside Block, Buzz brings employees and AI agents into a shared workspace. With Databricks Unity Gateway, employees who use Buzz can access frontier and open-weight models, experiment with different agent harnesses, and find the right combination based on the efficiency frontier for each task.

As AI agents become part of everyday work, Block’s teams needed a way to work with agents in the same place they work with each other. Block developed Buzz, an open source collaboration space where people and AI agents can work together in group discussions, focused conversations, and one-on-one exchanges.

Buzz brings agents into the same collaborative environment as employees. Users can create an agent, choose the model or coding harness behind it, and bring that agent into a conversation with colleagues. Rather than switching between different AI tools, teams can work with multiple agents in one place.

At Block, Databricks Unity Gateway helps power the Buzz experience by providing access to a broad selection of frontier and open-weight models through a single integration. That gives employees the flexibility to experiment with different models and match them to the work they're trying to accomplish.

Buzz gives people and AI agents a shared workspace to exchange information, contribute context, and work together on tasks. Employees can create AI agents, work with them individually or alongside colleagues, and bring others into ongoing work. For example, an employee can ask an agent to help with coding or analysis, while colleagues review its work, provide additional information, or ask follow-up questions.

Buzz includes its own built-in agent, which incorporates a lightweight version of Goose, and also supports other coding harnesses and tools. As an open source project, Buzz is model-agnostic and can be self-hosted, meaning it can run privately on your own network or system, giving users flexibility in how they deploy and configure their agents.

At Block, employees are using Buzz for coding, analytics, and other day-to-day work. Many bring agents into the same conversations where colleagues are already collaborating.

Buzz lets users choose the model or harness behind each agent. A coding task, an analytical question, and a lightweight everyday request may benefit from different models or agent harnesses. Instead of committing to a single model for every workflow, Buzz lets users make that choice when creating their agents.

Unity Gateway provides the model access layer for this experience. When employees create an agent in Buzz, they can select Databricks as their inference provider and choose from the models available through Unity Gateway. That includes frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, as well as select open-weight models, all accessible through a single integration.

This flexibility matters as new models become available and teams learn which ones work best for different tasks. Instead of designing every agent around the same model, employees can create a collection of specialized agents, each with its own model or harness, and bring them together in Buzz.

Model choice becomes even more interesting when multiple agents collaborate on the same task. Block has been experimenting with different combinations of models and agent harnesses to understand how they affect performance and cost. One approach its engineers have explored is using a more capable model to coordinate work across a team of agents powered by smaller, more efficient models.

The idea is straightforward because not every step of a complex task requires the most expensive model. A coordinating agent can take on the more demanding work, while other agents handle tasks suited to their capabilities. In Buzz, those interactions can take place within the same collaborative environment, where people can see how agents work with each other and participate in the work.

Block has also developed an internal approach to benchmarking these agent teams, giving its engineers a way to experiment with different configurations. This approach reflects a broader shift in how teams are thinking about AI development. The question is no longer just which single model performs best but how to combine models, harnesses, and agents to complete work effectively.

Buzz reflects a different way to think about AI at work. Rather than treating each agent as an individual tool, Block built an environment where people can create, collaborate with, and coordinate multiple agents in the same place.

With Unity Gateway providing access to frontier and open-weight models, Block employees can experiment with different combinations of models and harnesses to find what works best for each task, all within the collaborative Buzz experience.

Get started with Block Buzz and Unity Gateway

  • Try Block Buzz: Explore the open source project on GitHub and start building agents that work alongside your team.
  • Explore Databricks Unity Gateway: Learn how to access frontier and open-weight AI models through a single API for your own AI applications and agents.

Block Buzz is an open source collaboration workspace where employees and AI agents can work together in channels, threads, and direct messages. Users can create agents, choose their models or coding harnesses, and collaborate with multiple agents and colleagues in the same environment.

Block uses Databricks Unity Gateway to provide centralized access to frontier and open-weight AI models within Buzz. Employees can select Databricks as their inference provider and choose from available models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, through a single integration.

Enterprises can assign different models to AI agents based on task requirements, performance, and cost. With Buzz and Unity Gateway, Block employees can experiment with different combinations of models and agent harnesses rather than relying on one model for every workflow.

Multi-agent workflows allow teams to use different models for different parts of a task. For example, a more capable model can coordinate complex work while smaller, more efficient models handle simpler tasks. Block is experimenting with these configurations to understand how model and harness selection affects performance and cost.

Yes. Block Buzz is open source, model-agnostic, and can be self-hosted. It supports multiple models and agent harnesses, and organizations can integrate with Databricks Unity Gateway to access frontier and open-weight models through a single API.

entries.title: Air gapped, not data dark: how Bright Machines gives customers live factory dashboards without opening the plant
entries.summary: Bright Machines gives customers live, governed dashboards of their factory data without...
entries.content:
How Bright Machines streams factory changes out of air-gapped plants with Debezium, Apache Iceberg and Unity Catalog, so customers see live, governed dashboards with no inbound access to the plant

by Jitesh Soni, Anup Chatterjee, Bryan Whittington, Mark Loesel, Mauricio Caro, Caitlin Gordon and Rachel Musiker

  • Live factory data from an air-gapped plant: Bright Machines captures PostgreSQL changes at the edge with Debezium and writes them as Apache Iceberg. The data goes out over one auditable outbound path, and Databricks reads it in place through Unity Catalog federation with AWS Glue.
  • One governed platform replaces a nine-service pipeline: The old pipeline broke when schemas changed, failures went unnoticed and it had no real access controls. Now one Unity Catalog-governed platform serves role-based AI/BI Dashboards and zero-copy shares.
  • Results: Data can be queried in Databricks 1–2 minutes after it's written on the line, and dashboards refresh every 10 minutes. A heartbeat check catches a broken pipeline in under 30 minutes instead of days, and the first customer dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

Bright Machines gives customers live, governed dashboards of their factory data without opening any inbound access to its air-gapped plants. It captures PostgreSQL changes at the factory edge with Debezium, writes them as Apache Iceberg, sends them out over a single auditable outbound path, and reads them in place in Databricks through Unity Catalog federation. The first customer-visible dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

  • Problem: customers wanted factory data, and the only way to share it was reports rerun on-prem and sent over by email.
  • Solution: Debezium change data capture, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue, Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, AI/BI Dashboards and OpenSharing.
  • Result: nine loosely coupled services replaced by one governed platform plus one edge path, with zero inbound ports to the plant.
  • Freshness: a row committed on the line is queryable in Databricks in one to two minutes, and dashboards refresh every ten minutes.
  • Monitoring: a heartbeat check detects a broken pipeline in under thirty minutes, down from days.

Every time a customer visited one of our factory floors, the same thing happened. They would stand in front of the assembly dashboard, watch the line run, and ask for a copy of the data: yield by station, cycle time trends, downtime by cause, the genealogy of a batch.

We had all of it. We had built those dashboards for our own operations team, and they ran on the floor against the line databases. A customer could not access any of it directly over the internet. The plant is air gapped by design: no inbound access, one tightly controlled route out, and role-based access rules that restricted access in.

Each new report required data engineering to reshape data through multiple ETL jobs, costing hours to days of engineering time.

Bright Machines builds software-defined, automation-first production lines that run inside our customers' plants. Those plants are locked down by design: no inbound access, minimal outbound, and zero tolerance for risk. Each line runs a stack of on-premises services (our in-house MES, integrations with customer's MES, operator screens, robot workflow orchestrators, and the assembly dashboards) that all persist to PostgreSQL on the factory's on-prem cluster. The software team that runs this is a lean team and manages the data pipelines end to end as well as the data applications software stack. The data drives various KPI dashboards, finance reporting, operations, quality, vendor component quality, NCR tracking, genealogy, OEE and the downtime and cycle-time analysis behind every shift.

On our first attempt to solve this problem, we rebuilt a cloud copy of each factory database from application events, across nine loosely coupled services. On the factory floor the picture was fine. Everything off the floor was the problem with this complex architecture and pipeline.

The nine services were a message broker, a custom shoveler, a queue, object storage, few serverless functions, a cloud relational database, a scheduler, an ETL pipeline, and a popular open source BI tool with very basic RBAC support.

The pipeline failed for these reasons:

  • Schema Evolution. Schemas changed often, and the pipeline silently dropped changed data unless the ETL jobs were updated every time an on-prem dashboard or schema changed.
  • Missing monitoring. The pipeline had failures and the dead-letter queues were a pain to monitor, so missed or duplicated events went unnoticed.
  • Data validation. Once data landed in a bucket, nobody could say with confidence if it was accurate and from the right source.
  • Data Governance. Having proper governance and role based access controls over views and data that we shared.

Fixing all the above features needed rearchitecting from the ground up.

In addition to the above reasons these constraints also shaped the new design:

Security Model. No inbound connectivity to the plant, and all access auditable.

Governance we could demonstrate. A customer would see exactly what their role allowed on the floor, and we had to be able to prove the appropriate limits were in place.

Freshness in minutes. A dashboard view that is on prem would be visible in a few minutes over the internet with the same data.

The new architecture:

Bright Machines chose edge change data capture with Unity Catalog federation because it was the only option where no compute outside a customer's and/or Bright Machines' own accounts touched factory data before governance is applied.

Our criteria, in order: access control that matched what was already enforced on the floor, one outbound auditable path we could explain to any security team, minute-level freshness, and open formats at the edge.

We worked through the options with our Databricks solutions architect before writing any code. The two obvious ones were Lakeflow Connect ingesting directly from PostgreSQL, and a Postgres export picked up by Auto Loader. Both would have been faster to stand up. Our threat model followed the rule that data can be pushed out, but nothing outside can reach in. A pull-based ingestion pattern needs a network path from the cloud to the factory database, and running ingestion in an environment outside the accounts where the data resided. So the question became: how do we get the same governed result while keeping every piece that touches raw factory data inside environments we own?

The answer was to flip the direction. Capture changes at the edge, land them in an open format, push them out over one auditable path, and let Databricks read them in place.

We proved it on a replicated line, similar to that of a production site, with two engineers over about six weeks. The bar had two parts. First, a row committed on the line had to be queryable in under five minutes with no inbound port opened. Second, a customer principal had to see exactly the tables and dashboards their role allowed, and nothing else.

The deciding factor was that Databricks already enforced the security model that aligned with ours: Unity Catalog for who can see what, and OpenSharing to publish governed tables without copies. Going in, we worried that governance on federated tables would not be strict enough for the audit. It was strict, and the strictness that tripped us up during cutover is the same strictness we rely on now.

Data leaves the factory in five steps, over a single outbound path, and Databricks reads it in place without a copy job. Operators keep the on-prem assembly dashboard, because they need real time. Databricks cloud serves customers and internal teams.

Capture at the edge with Debezium. Debezium Server tails the PostgreSQL replication slot and writes an append-only Apache Iceberg change log to a local object store. If the WAN drops, the backlog becomes objects on the floor, not write-ahead log piling up on the production database.

Send it out over one path. A single edge component copies each object to a bucket in the site's cloud account. It is the only outbound data path from the plant, and its credentials can write to that one bucket and nothing else. Cross-account replication carries the objects to the analytics account.

Federate it into Unity Catalog. The Iceberg tables are registered in AWS Glue, and Unity Catalog federates Glue as a read-only catalog. That makes over a hundred tables across factory PostgreSQL databases queryable in Databricks with no copy.

Model it in Databricks SQL. Bronze views collapse the change log to the current state. A Lakeflow Job rebuilds silver models every ten minutes, all in SQL and deployed from Git with Databricks Asset Bundles.

Serve it with dashboards and OpenSharing. Multiple AI/BI Dashboards read processed data from the silver layer with role-based permissions. This allowed external customers and internal teams to all see the same numbers. OpenSharing allows the same copy of data to be shared securely to our customers.

Registering the tables in AWS Glue lets Bright Machines control exactly when each table moves forward. A change log on object storage is a stream of new metadata files. A small function advances each table's pointer in Glue only when a new metadata file has fully replicated, and only forward. Glue holds the pointer, Unity Catalog holds the permissions, and Databricks only ever reads the version we have validated.

Use a heartbeat. When a line stops for a shift change, no new rows arrive, and that looks exactly like a broken pipeline. Row counts cannot tell the two extremes apart.

Debezium updates a one-row heartbeat table in each source database every five minutes, whether or not the line is running. That update travels the same path as production data. The first task of the Lakeflow Job checks the heartbeat, and if any is more than thirty minutes old, the task fails and the whole job goes red. Dashboards keep showing the last good data instead of presenting stale data as current.

We phased it in four steps: 1.) a pilot on a PoC line, 2.) going live with the highest-value production line, 3.) a parallel run against the old snapshot path to check row for row parity, and 4.) a hard cutover of the dashboards for customers.

What surprised us. Scale showed up in the wrong dimension. We moved a few 100 gigabytes a day, but as hundreds of thousands of small objects, so every design decision ended up being about object rate rather than dictated by bytes.

What we would do differently. Build the reconciliation pass on day one. A sync driven by create events never goes back for an object it missed, and nothing downstream notices until a query touches it.

The focus of those customer visits changed. Nobody asks for a copy of the dashboard any more, because they already have it, under the roles available to them. A customer analyst opens the Quality dashboard from their desk and sees the same numbers the line lead sees on the floor, within about ten minutes of them happening. We never run a report. The first customer-visible dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

Five lessons for anyone sharing data from a locked-down site:

  • Start from the security model you already have. Our data governance requirements defined the roles and restrictions. We picked the platform that enforced exactly those, rather than approximating them.
  • Design the one path out first, and buffer behind it. A single auditable egress makes every later conversation with a security team manageable. Buffering at the edge means a WAN blip never becomes a production database incident.
  • Keep control of when a table moves forward. A catalog hop you own, with a guard on the pointer, means the lakehouse only ever sees a version you have validated.
  • Build the data once and let permissions do the rest. Maintaining a customer version and an operations version of every report was what ate the hours.
  • Assert freshness on a heartbeat, not on row counts. No new rows means the line is idle. No new heartbeat means the pipeline is broken.

Now that the data is governed and accessible, the next step is to make this more accessible to AI features through natural language analytics with Genie, custom AI agents for operations, and predictive analytics that turn factory data into forward-looking decisions.

Having custom AI agents for operational analytics and investigations. The people who work on those lines - operators, quality engineers, maintenance techs have domain expertise but aren't SQL users. Custom AI agents (via Databricks Apps or Agent Bricks) could let a line lead ask "Why did station 4 have higher downtime this shift?" Bright Machines provided knowledge docs along with operational data could get an answer grounded in the same governed silver data. This is the "improve the bottom line" play — reducing the time from question to action on the factory floor.

Q: Can Databricks be used with an air-gapped factory?

Yes. Bright Machines keeps zero inbound ports open to the plant for data. Changes are captured inside the factory and pushed out over one auditable outbound path, and Databricks reads the resulting Apache Iceberg tables in place through Unity Catalog federation.

Q: How fresh is the factory data in Databricks?

A row committed on the line is queryable in Databricks in one to two minutes at steady state. Silver models and dashboards refresh every ten minutes. Operators who need real time views keep using the on-prem assembly dashboards.

Q: How do customers access the data?

In two ways: AI/BI Dashboards with role-based permissions integrated with Bright Machine’s SSO Federation, and additional capability to provide OpenSharing access, which publishes zero copy governed silver tables to customers with Databricks accounts.

Q: What replaced the old nine-service pipeline?

One governed platform, Databricks, plus a single edge path made up of Debezium, a local object store and one sync component. Bronze views, silver models, the job, the dashboards and the shares are all deployed from one Databricks Asset Bundle.

Q: This design was specifically built on AWS, does the design work on Azure or Google Cloud?

The cloud-specific parts are the edge sync target, the cross-account replication and the catalog hop. Everything on the Databricks side is the same on any cloud, so moving it is a change to a few resources rather than a rebuild.

Q: How long did it take?

The proof of concept took about six weeks with two engineers. The first customer-visible dashboard went live about two months after kickoff.

Want to share governed data from locked-down sites without opening inbound access? Learn how Unity Catalog federates Apache Iceberg tables from AWS Glue, or talk to your Databricks account team about your architecture.
